newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels to Fujimori no talks, no solution.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels to Fujimori no talks, no solution.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 74 VIP captives at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima told President Alberto Fujimori on Saturday that without talks, there will be no solution to the country's 18-day hostage crisis.

The rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) sneaked onto the roof of the residence under cover of darkness and unfurled three banners in which they replied to an uncompromising speech by Fujimori two days ago.
"Mr Fujimori, with arrogant declarations and without dialogue, there will never be a solution," one of the banners said. The rebels also erected an MRTA flag.
The other two banners, unfurled at about 4.30 a.m. (0930 GMT), read as follows:
"Mothers, wives and children of our prisoners are also waiting for their freedom. Peace for all Peruvians", and
"Today's Peru -- 13 million Peruvians in extreme poverty. Where is the progress?"
The rebels, who stormed the residence on Dec. 17 during a reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito, are demanding the release of some 400 MRTA members from Peruvian prisons.
Fujimori on Thursday rejected the rebels' claim to be fighting poverty in Peru and condemned them as "terrorists" bent on violence. He has ruled out freeing any MRTA prisoners.
The hostage crisis entered its 18th day on Saturday amid increasing signs that it will not be over any time soon.

In Tokyo, Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said on Saturday that the prospects of winning the release of the high-level hostages were now worse than at any time since the seizure of the residence.
Hashimoto said at a news briefing that with no talks taking place between the government and the MRTA, "the situation is more serious than ever before."
"Dialogue began before the new year between the MRTA and the Peruvian government but now it has reached an impasse," he said.
Earlier on Saturday, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was "not optimistic" about ending the standoff.
"I am not optimistic about the situation, seeing as the number of hostages has been reduced to a level where it is easy for the terrorists to control them," Hashimoto told reporters.
Speculation that a deal could be cut to release some of the remaining hostages was also quickly snuffed out by Japan.
"I would like to make it plain once again that neither Peru nor Japan have any intention of paying a ransom," Hiroshi Hashimoto said.

The only activity at the besieged residence on Friday was the usual shuttling to and fro of Red Cross workers, taking in food, medicines and, for the first time, books for the hostages. They promised to send in "primitive" cleaning materials on Saturday.
There was no sign of the government's negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo.

Following last week's first face-to-face meeting between Palermo and the guerrillas, Fujimori has kept his negotiator out of the building despite MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa's assurance that "the doors are open."
The rebels have not freed any hostages since Wednesday when seven were released following a visit by Juan Luis Cipriani, bishop of the Andean province of Ayacucho.
Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori, has not been to the diplomatic compound since.

While Fujimori has found replacements for government positions held by some of the hostages, the jungle-trained rebels, in remarks by their European representative in Hamburg, Germany, said they could withstand the harsh conditions inside the residence even if their prisoners could not.

Without explanation, Fujimori removed from their posts on Thursday two police generals captured by the rebels -- the head of Peru's anti-terrorism force and the chief of national security. He also swore in a new Supreme Court president to replace Moises Pantoja, another hostage.
The remaining captives included Fujimori's brother, two ambassadors, top Peruvian government and security force officials, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.

Fujimori's political position appeared more precarious on Friday after media reports that Peru's Constitutional Court had ruled as illegal a potential bid for a third term of office in 2000. Fujimori is widely believed to want a third term as president.
Officially, the court's magistrates said they had made a decision on Friday but would delay announcing it until the hostage crisis was over.
